	Petitioner Douglas Van Essen filed this Contested Case Petition on September 20, 2010.  After discovery and a hearing on Respondent’s Motion to Dismiss, this case came before the undersigned on March 29, 2011, for a hearing on the merits.

	At the hearing, the parties agreed the evidence relevant to Petitioner’s claims is undisputed, and that this Petitioner could be resolved through summary judgment.  Petitioner filed a Motion for Summary Judgment with attached exhibits, and Respondent filed a counter-Motion for Summary Judgment against Petitioner.

	After hearing oral argument and reviewing the parties’ Motions and attached evidence, the undersigned grants Petitioner’s Motion for Summary Judgment and denies Respondent’s counter-Motion for Summary Judgment, for the reasons set out below:

	I.	Factual Background

	Petitioner Douglas Van Essen was employed for more than ten consecutive years as the Executive Director of Respondent North Carolina Board of Cosmetic Arts Examiners.   Respondent terminated Petitioner in October 2008. At the time of his October 2008 termination, Petitioner’s position was not exempt from the State Personnel Act.  N.C. Gen. Stat. §88B-6(b).  Petitioner filed a first Contested Case Petition, claiming he was terminated without just cause.  During the pendency of that Petition, effective August 26, 2009, Section 88B-6(b) of the Cosmetic Arts Act was amended to make the Executive Director position exempt from the State Personnel Act.  On April 22, 2010, the State Personnel Commission entered a Decision favorable to Van Essen and ordered his reinstatement.

	On May 27, 2010, Respondent reinstated Petitioner to his Executive Director position and then immediately terminated him.  The Executive Director position was exempt from the State Personnel Act at the time of the second termination.  Respondent admits it did not have just cause for the May 2010 termination.  Respondent notified Petitioner of the decision in a May 27, 2010 letter.  Respondent’s letter did not indicate whether Petitioner had any right to be hired in an alternate position, under N.C. Gen. Stat. §126-5(e).

	After the second termination, Petitioner applied for jobs with the State and asked Respondent to comply with Section 126-5(e)(2) and reinstate him to another position.  Respondent has not hired Petitioner in another job or placed him in another job in State government.  Respondent informed Petitioner it would not comply with Section 126-5(e)(2).

	II. 	Discussion - Section 126-5(e)(2) claim

	Section 126-5(e)(2) states:

An exempt employee may be transferred, demoted or separated from his or her position by the department head authorized to designate the exempt position except . . .

(2) when an employee has 10 years or more cumulative service, including the immediately preceding 12 months, in subject positions prior to placement in an exempt position is removed from an exempt position, for reasons other than just cause, the employee shall be reassigned to a subject position . . .

Subsection (2) of Section 126-5(e) applies directly to Petitioner’s situation, since Petitioner is an employee with 10 years of more cumulative service, since he was in a position subject to the State Personnel Act prior to being placed in an exempt position, and since he was removed from an exempt position on May 27, 2010 for reasons other than just cause.  Petitioner thus has met the pre-requisites for coverage under Section 126-5(e)(2) and is entitled to reassignment to a subject position.

	Respondent has contended that Petitioner is not covered under Section 126-5(e)(2), arguing that the first paragraph of Section 126-5(e), referring to termination by a “department head authorized to designate the exempt position,” is intended to limit those individuals entitled to Section 126-5(e) reinstatement only to those whose positions were made exempt by the Governor or a department head. Respondent’s position is unsupported by the wording of Section 126-5(e) and is without merit. In Carrington v. Brown, 136 N.C.App. 554, 525, S.E.2d 230 (2000), the Court of Appeals addressed the significance of this prefatory language and held that it was employed to denote who has authority to fire an exempt employee who may then, under subparagraphs (1) or (2), be entitled to additional entitlements to reinstatement.  The Court of Appeals further held that the “department head authorized to designate the exempt position” phrase, if read literally, would mean that only department heads within the Council of State could terminate individuals in exempt positions, since under N.C.  Gen. Stat. §126-5(d)(2) only Council of State department heads have authority to designate positions exempt; for other departments, that authority lies with the Governor, N.C. Gen. Stat. §126-d(1), or the legislature, see e.g. N.C. Gen. Stat. §126-c.  The Court held the legislature could not have intended that absurd result, and ruled the “department head” language must be read expansively to include terminations from all exempt positions.  Accordingly, the undersigned believes that language relied upon by Respondent does not bar Petitioner from protection under Section 126-5(e(2).  Petitioner is entitled to reinstatement under that provision, and to all other remedies spelled out under the North Carolina Administrative Code.

	Accordingly, Petitioner’s Motion for Summary Judgment is granted, and Respondent’s counter-Motion is denied.

NOTICE

	The agency making the final decision in this contested case is required to give each party an opportunity to file exceptions to this decision, and to present written arguments to those in the agency who will make the final decision.  N. C. Gen. Stat. § 150B-36(a).

	In accordance with N.C. Gen. Stat. § 150B-36 the agency shall adopt each finding of fact contained in the Administrative Law Judge’s decision unless the finding is clearly contrary to the preponderance of the admissible evidence.  For each finding of fact not adopted by the agency, the agency shall set forth separately and in detail the reasons for not adopting the finding of fact and the evidence in the record relied upon by the agency in not adopting the finding of fact.  For each new finding of fact made by the agency that is not contained in the Administrative Law Judge’s decision, the agency shall set forth separately and in detail the evidence in the record relied upon by the agency in making the finding of fact.

The agency that will make the final decision in this case is the North Carolina State of Cosmetic Arts Examiners.

	IT IS SO ORDERED.

	This 29th  day of April, 2011.
